response: It makes sense that waiting without an explanation left you feeling unimportant, and that B seeming annoyed on arrival made the evening harder. The delay itself was caused by a cancelled train, which you had not heard about, so the lateness does not by itself show that B was trying to dismiss the dinner. What you felt while waiting is still real. It may help to tell B that you needed a message, and to ask what the arrival felt like from their side, rather than treating either reading as settled.

B, it sounds like the evening was stressful. You were anxious on the platform, wanted to make dinner, and tried to send a message without knowing if it got through. Arriving at 7:30 after a cancelled train, then finding A unwilling to talk, would feel isolating. The delay itself is explained by the cancellation, not by a wish to hurt A. It may help to tell A what you felt and that you tried to reach them, and to ask what silence meant for them. You both deserve a calm conversation about the missed connection and how to handle delays next time.

It sounds like you both had a hard evening and were left with very different pictures of what happened. A, waiting without any word made the delay feel personal, and that hurt. B, you were anxious, trying to get there, and unsure whether your message arrived. The cancellation explains the lateness, but it does not erase how either of you felt. When you talk, it may help to separate what happened from what it seemed to mean: A can say how the silence landed, and B can say what the platform and the arrival were like. Listening before explaining could make room for both of you.

You both seem to have left dinner with hurt that the other person did not fully see. B, your account is of anxiety, a real wish to arrive, and uncertainty about whether a message got through. A, you describe waiting without news, feeling unimportant, and reading B's late arrival and manner as a lack of care. The shared facts place the missed train outside either of your intentions, which does not erase how the wait felt. It may help to tell each other what you experienced and what you needed—an update, reassurance, or a calmer greeting—without treating the other's feeling as proof of motive.

It may help to tell B what you felt and what greeting you would like, and to ask what the time alone was for, rather than treating anger as already known.

A, your feeling of rejection is understandable when someone you live with goes straight to another room, and nothing in what you shared shows an agreed greeting. B's account, though, describes work noise, overload, and a wish for a short quiet interval so they could meet your needs afterward. That account does not say anger, and it does not say B wanted the relationship to end. B, twenty minutes alone can still read as distance even with a caring intention. A and B, the shared facts show B spent twenty minutes alone after coming home, and you had no explicit greeting agreement. B describes feeling overloaded by work noise and wanting a quiet interval before engaging with A's needs. A describes feeling rejected and reads B's withdrawal as anger. Those are different experiences of the same moment, and neither account establishes that B was angry or wanted the relationship to end. It may help to separate impact from intent: A can name the rejection without treating it as proof of B's motive, and B can acknowledge the effect of the delay even if the purpose was recovery. A short check-in after such pauses could reduce this gap.

A, it is understandable that the dishes still sitting there felt like being taken for granted, given the agreement that B would wash them. What is established is that agreement and that the dishes remained overnight. You have not asked B what happened, so the idea that B expected you to do them is an assumption, not a known fact. A calm check-in about what got in the way, and how you want to handle it next time, would let B explain and keep this from hardening into silent resentment.

B, it makes sense that a long, important call pulled your attention and that you felt annoyed when the dishes were still waiting. Forgetting after a demanding conversation is understandable, and wanting A to recognize that the call mattered is fair. At the same time, you had agreed to wash them that evening, and they remained overnight. A reasonable next step is to acknowledge the missed agreement directly, wash the dishes, and say what you can do differently next time, such as setting a reminder before calls or renegotiating if something urgent comes up. Asking A to understand the call does not replace following through.

A and B, it makes sense that this felt bigger than dirty dishes. A, feeling taken for granted is understandable when an agreement is not met and you only see the sink in the morning, though you did not yet hear what happened. B, forgetting after an important call explains the miss, but annoyance and asking A to simply understand does not replace the agreement you made. The dishes stayed overnight; that part is not in dispute. A short check-in about what each of you felt, and how you will handle a similar conflict next time, would do more than either of you guessing the other's intent.

Both of you seem to be reacting to more than dirty dishes. B, your account says you felt annoyed, agreed to wash them, and then forgot after a long, important call. That explains the miss, but it does not remove the agreement A was counting on. A, you felt taken for granted when you saw the sink in the morning and assumed B expected you to finish the job, yet you did not ask what happened. A brief conversation can separate the forgotten task from the meaning each of you gave it. Start with the agreement, the call, and the assumption, then decide together how to handle a similar evening next time.

It makes sense that you felt disappointed after expecting Saturday to be time together. What the facts show, though, is that you and B had not agreed to spend that afternoon together, and each of you made separate plans. Your assumption explains the hurt, but it does not by itself establish that B planned the afternoon in order to avoid you. That motive is still unknown. A calm conversation about what each of you expected, and how you want to handle unscheduled time, would be more useful than treating the avoidance idea as settled.

It makes sense that you felt surprised if you believed you were each making separate plans, and the shared facts do line up with that: you had not agreed to spend Saturday afternoon together, and you both made other plans. Still, calling A always sensitive may widen the disagreement rather than explain it. Surprise on both sides can happen when expectations were never spelled out. It may help to say what you understood, ask what A expected, and agree on how to handle overlapping free time next time, without treating either of you as the problem.

You each seem to be reacting to a different picture of Saturday. A, disappointment follows naturally from assuming the afternoon was yours together, but that assumption was not a shared agreement. B, surprise fits if you thought separate plans were already understood. What is not settled is motive: feeling avoided is real for A, yet the facts do not show that B planned in order to stay away. Calling A always sensitive also goes beyond what is shown and can shut the conversation down. Naming the missed expectation, without assigning intent, may be the clearer next step.

You both seem to have held different expectations for Saturday afternoon. The shared facts show that each of you made separate plans and that you had not agreed to spend that time together. A, your disappointment followed from assuming the afternoon was shared and from reading B's plans as avoidance. B, you felt surprised because you believed separate plans were understood, and you experience A as sensitive. A, the silence understandably left you worried, especially when you could not tell whether the message had been read. That uncertainty can easily feel like rejection even when it is not. B describes the phone being in a bag during work and wanting to focus, while not wanting A to feel ignored. That gap between silence and intention is understandable on both sides. A brief note when you can, even if delayed, may reduce worry. It also helps to say when focus time is needed, so unread silence is less likely to be taken as anger.

You said you wanted to leave and that you felt afraid when you could not. The facts given also say you asked to leave, there was only one doorway, and you were unable to leave for five minutes. Wanting space during an argument is reasonable, and not agreeing to stay matters. Being kept from leaving can be frightening. You do not have to keep arguing while you cannot get out. If you feel unsafe or this keeps happening, consider telling someone you trust or contacting a local support service.

B, it makes sense that you felt panicked and wanted the argument finished rather than left hanging. Wanting a resolution is not the same as being entitled to keep someone in the room. After A said they wanted to leave, you stood in the only doorway and A could not get out for five minutes. That blocked exit is the part that matters most here. You can ask to keep talking, name the panic, and still move. A pause, with a clear time to return, respects both the need to resolve things and A's choice to step away.

A, wanting space and feeling afraid when you could not leave is understandable; you did not agree to stay, and an unfinished argument did not require you to remain. B, panic about the conversation ending is a real feeling, but blocking the only doorway after being asked to move was not a fair way to seek resolution. You can pause, separate, and return only when each person is free to leave. If this pattern continues, outside support can help you set safer boundaries.

A, wanting space and feeling afraid when you could not leave is understandable. You asked to leave and did not agree to stay. B, feeling panicked and wanting a resolution explains your urgency, but it does not justify blocking the only doorway for five minutes. A could not leave, and that matters more than finishing the talk in that moment. You can both pause, give each other room, and continue only if leaving remains possible and both choose to talk. The freedom to step away has to come first.
